questions.question: What does Flyway do when the application starts?
options: It deletes the database and recreates it
It runs the migration files that have not been applied yet, in version order
It converts Java entities into SQL on every start
It copies data to a backup server
questions.explanation: Flyway compares the files with its history table and runs only the new migrations in order.

questions.question: Which file name is a valid Flyway versioned migration?
questions.explanation: The pattern is a capital V, the version, two underscores, the description and .sql.

questions.question: The migration folder holds V1__create_member.sql and V2__add_phone.sql. On a database where V1 already ran, the app starts. What does Flyway run?
options: Nothing, because the history table exists
questions.explanation: V1 is already recorded in flyway_schema_history, so only the new V2 migration runs.

questions.question: A developer fixes a typo inside V1__create_member.sql, which already ran on the test server. The next startup fails. Why?
options: Flyway stores a checksum of each applied file and the changed file no longer matches
V1 files may only be edited on Mondays
questions.explanation: An applied migration must never change, so the fix belongs in a new migration such as V3.

questions.question: A project uses Flyway but keeps spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update in production. What is the risk?
options: Hibernate and Flyway both change the schema, so the tables can drift from the migration files
Entities can no longer be saved
questions.explanation: Two tools editing one schema causes drift, so use validate or none when Flyway owns the schema.
